    35→| Command execution time | Completes validation of a typical config file (under 1000 lines) in under 1 second |
    36→
    37→## 3. Stakeholders & Users
    38→
    39→### 3.1 User Types
    40→
    41→| User Type | Description | Interaction |
    42→|-----------|-------------|-------------|
    43→| Developer | A developer using the project's CLI tools to validate YAML configuration files | Invokes the validator command from the terminal, passing a file path or piped input |
    44→| CI/CD Pipeline | An automated process that needs to gate deployments on configuration correctness | Invokes the validator command and relies on the exit code to determine pass/fail |
    45→
    46→### 3.2 Stakeholder Interests
    47→
    48→| Stakeholder | Interest |
    49→|-------------|----------|
    50→| Project Maintainers | Keep the project dependency-free; ensure new commands follow existing code patterns |
    51→| End Users | Receive clear, actionable feedback about YAML validity without installing extra tools |
    52→
    53→## 4. Scope Definition
    54→
    55→### 4.1 In Scope
    56→
    57→- A command that can be invoked to validate a YAML file provided as a file path argument.
    58→- Reporting of validation results: valid or invalid with error details (line number, description of the problem).
    59→- Appropriate exit codes: zero for valid YAML, non-zero for invalid YAML or errors.
    60→- Support for standard YAML syntax (mappings, sequences, scalars, multi-line strings, comments, anchors/aliases).
    61→- Unit tests covering valid YAML, invalid YAML, edge cases (empty input, non-existent file).
    62→
    63→### 4.2 Out of Scope
    64→
    65→- YAML schema validation (validating against a specific schema or structure beyond syntax).
    66→- YAML linting or style enforcement (indentation preferences, key ordering, etc.).
    67→- YAML transformation, formatting, or pretty-printing.
    68→- Support for YAML stream documents (multiple documents separated by `---`) beyond basic detection.
    69→- Interactive or GUI-based validation.
    70→- Adding any new runtime or development dependencies to the project.
    71→
    72→### 4.3 Assumptions
    73→
    74→- Bun's runtime environment provides sufficient built-in capabilities (file I/O, string processing) to implement a basic YAML syntax validator without external libraries.
    75→- The validator targets YAML 1.2 core schema syntax at a practical level; exhaustive compliance with every edge case of the YAML 1.2 specification is not required for an MVP.
    76→- Users will provide input as a file path argument to the command.
    77→
    78→## 5. Functional Requirements
    79→
    80→### FR-001: Validate YAML File from File Path
    81→**Priority**: Must Have
    82→**User Type**: Developer, CI/CD Pipeline
    83→**Requirement**: A user must be able to invoke the validator by providing a file path as a command-line argument. The system reads the file and reports whether its contents are valid YAML.
    84→**Rationale**: File-based validation is the primary use case for checking configuration files.
    85→**Acceptance Criteria**:
    86→- AC-1: Given a valid YAML file path, the command outputs a success message indicating the file is valid.
    87→- AC-2: Given an invalid YAML file path (malformed YAML), the command outputs an error message describing the syntax problem.
    88→- AC-3: Given a non-existent file path, the command outputs a clear error message stating the file was not found.
    89→
    90→### FR-002: Provide Meaningful Error Messages
    91→**Priority**: Must Have
    92→**User Type**: Developer
    93→**Requirement**: When YAML is invalid, the validator must report the approximate location (line number) of the error and a human-readable description of the problem.
    94→**Rationale**: Developers need actionable feedback to fix YAML errors efficiently; a simple "invalid" message is not sufficient.
    95→**Acceptance Criteria**:
    96→- AC-1: Error output includes the line number where the problem was detected.
    97→- AC-2: Error output includes a description of what was expected vs. what was found (e.g., "unexpected indentation", "invalid character").
    98→
    99→### FR-003: Return Appropriate Exit Codes
   100→**Priority**: Must Have
   101→**User Type**: CI/CD Pipeline
   102→**Requirement**: The command must return exit code 0 when the input YAML is valid, and a non-zero exit code when the input is invalid or an error occurs.
   103→**Rationale**: Automated pipelines rely on exit codes to determine success or failure without parsing output text.
   104→**Acceptance Criteria**:
   105→- AC-1: Exit code is 0 when the provided YAML is syntactically valid.
   106→- AC-2: Exit code is 1 (or another non-zero value) when the provided YAML is syntactically invalid.
   107→- AC-3: Exit code is non-zero when an operational error occurs (e.g., file not found, permission denied).
   108→
   109→### FR-004: Handle Edge Cases Gracefully
   110→**Priority**: Should Have
   111→**User Type**: Developer
   112→**Requirement**: The validator should handle edge cases such as empty files, files containing only comments, and files containing only whitespace without crashing or producing misleading results.
   113→**Rationale**: Real-world YAML files may be empty or contain only comments; the validator should not report these as errors.
   114→**Acceptance Criteria**:
   115→- AC-1: An empty file is treated as valid YAML (an empty document is valid per the YAML specification).
   116→- AC-2: A file containing only YAML comments is treated as valid YAML.
   117→- AC-3: A file containing only whitespace is treated as valid YAML.
   118→- AC-4: The command does not crash or produce a stack trace for any of these edge cases.
   119→
   120→### FR-005: No New Dependencies
   121→**Priority**: Must Have
   122→**User Type**: Project Maintainers
   123→**Requirement**: The validator must be implemented using only the existing project dependencies (Bun built-ins, TypeScript). No new entries may be added to `dependencies` or `devDependencies` in `package.json`.
   124→**Rationale**: The project follows a zero-external-dependency philosophy. The feature request explicitly states "without adding new deps."
   125→**Acceptance Criteria**:
   126→- AC-1: The `package.json` file has no new entries in `dependencies` or `devDependencies` after the feature is implemented.
   127→- AC-2: No `node_modules` additions beyond what already exists.
   128→
   129→### FR-006: Validate Common YAML Constructs
   130→**Priority**: Should Have
   131→**User Type**: Developer
   132→**Requirement**: The validator should correctly identify the validity of common YAML constructs including key-value mappings, sequences (lists), nested structures, quoted strings, multi-line strings (literal and folded block scalars), and comments.
   133→**Rationale**: These are the most frequently used YAML features in configuration files, and the validator must handle them to be practically useful.
   134→**Acceptance Criteria**:
   135→- AC-1: A file with nested key-value mappings is correctly validated.
   136→- AC-2: A file with sequences (both block and flow style) is correctly validated.
   137→- AC-3: A file with multi-line strings (using `|` or `>`) is correctly validated.
   138→- AC-4: A file with inline comments is correctly validated.
   139→
   140→## 6. Non-Functional Requirements
   141→
   142→### 6.1 Performance Expectations
   143→
   144→| Expectation | Target |
   145→|-------------|--------|
   146→| Validation of a file under 1000 lines | Completes in under 1 second |
   147→| Validation of a file under 100 lines | Completes in under 200 milliseconds |
   148→
   149→### 6.2 Security Requirements
   150→
   151→- The command must only read the file specified; it must not write to, modify, or delete any files.
   152→- The command must not execute or evaluate any content within the YAML file.
   153→
   154→### 6.3 Usability Requirements
   155→
   156→- The command must provide a `--help` flag (or equivalent) that describes usage.
   157→- Error messages must be written in plain language, not raw parser internals.
   158→- Output should be suitable for terminal display (no excessive verbosity for valid files).
   159→
   160→### 6.4 Compliance Requirements
   161→
   162→- No additional compliance requirements beyond the zero-dependency constraint.
   163→
   164→## 7. User Stories
   165→
   166→### STORY-001: Validate a Configuration File
   167→**As a** developer
   168→**I want to** run a command that checks my YAML configuration file for syntax errors
   169→**So that** I can catch mistakes before they cause failures in my application or deployment pipeline.
   170→
   171→**Acceptance Scenarios**:
   172→- GIVEN a YAML file with correct syntax, WHEN I run the validator command with the file path, THEN I see a message confirming the file is valid and the process exits with code 0.
   173→- GIVEN a YAML file with a missing colon after a key, WHEN I run the validator command with the file path, THEN I see an error message indicating the line and nature of the problem and the process exits with a non-zero code.
   174→
   175→### STORY-002: Gate a CI Pipeline on YAML Validity
   176→**As a** CI/CD pipeline

   178→**So that** deployments are blocked when configuration files contain syntax errors.
   179→
   180→**Acceptance Scenarios**:
   181→- GIVEN a valid YAML configuration file, WHEN the validator is invoked in a pipeline step, THEN the step succeeds (exit code 0).
   182→- GIVEN an invalid YAML configuration file, WHEN the validator is invoked in a pipeline step, THEN the step fails (non-zero exit code) and the error details are visible in the pipeline log.

--- rp1_run_id: eee8570b-4105-40b6-97a1-404dd9f40750 --- # Technical Design: Simple YAML Validator Command **Feature ID**: add a simple yaml validator command without adding new deps **Version**: 1.0.0 **Status**: Draft **Created**: 2026-04-06 ## 1. Design Overview This design introduces a lightweight, zero-dependency YAML syntax validator as a new CLI command in the rp1-eval-project. The validator reads a YAML file by path, checks its contents for syntactic correctness using a custom line-by-line state-tracking parser, and reports clear success or failure with actionable error messages and appropriate exit codes. The implementation adds three new files following existing project conventions: a core validator module with pure functions, a CLI entry point, and co-located tests. No external dependencies are introduced. ```mermaid graph LR A["CLI Entry Point
src/validate-yaml.ts"] --> B["YAML Validator
src/yaml-validator.ts"] A --> C["File System
Bun.file()"] A --> D["Process
process.argv / process.exit"] B --> E["Validation Result"] E --> F["Console Output"] ``` ## 2. Architecture The feature follows the project's existing simple script-based architecture pattern. It adds a new entry point alongside the existing `src/index.ts` and a new utility module alongside `src/utils.ts`. ### 2.1 Component Architecture ```mermaid graph TB subgraph "New Files" CLI["src/validate-yaml.ts
(CLI Entry Point)"] VAL["src/yaml-validator.ts
(Core Validator Logic)"] TEST["src/yaml-validator.test.ts
(Tests)"] end subgraph "Existing Files (Unchanged)" IDX["src/index.ts"] UTL["src/utils.ts"] UTLT["src/utils.test.ts"] end subgraph "Bun Runtime" FS["Bun.file()"] PROC["process.argv / process.exit"] end CLI --> VAL CLI --> FS CLI --> PROC TEST --> VAL ``` ### 2.2 Command Flow Sequence ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant User participant CLI as validate-yaml.ts participant FS as File System participant VAL as yaml-validator.ts User->>CLI: bun run validate-yaml CLI->>CLI: Parse arguments (--help, file path) alt --help flag or no arguments CLI->>User: Print usage info, exit(0) or exit(1) end CLI->>FS: Bun.file(path).text() alt File not found or unreadable CLI->>User: Error message, exit(1) end FS-->>CLI: file contents (string) CLI->>VAL: validateYaml(contents) VAL-->>CLI: ValidationResult alt Valid YAML CLI->>User: Success message, exit(0) else Invalid YAML CLI->>User: Error with line number + description, exit(1) end ``` ## 3. Detailed Design ### 3.1 Core Types ```typescript // src/yaml-validator.ts /** Result of a YAML validation operation. */ interface ValidationResult { valid: boolean; errors: ValidationError[]; } /** A single validation error with location and description. */ interface ValidationError { line: number; message: string; } ``` ### 3.2 Validator Module (`src/yaml-validator.ts`) The module exports a single primary function: ```typescript export function validateYaml(content: string): ValidationResult ``` **Approach**: Line-by-line state-tracking parser. The validator processes the YAML content line by line, maintaining state about: - Current indentation level and indentation stack - Whether we are inside a block scalar (`|` or `>`) - Whether we are inside a flow context (`[...]` or `{...}`) - Anchor/alias tracking (names referenced by `*` must have a corresponding `&` definition) **Validation checks performed per line:** | Check | Description | |-------|-------------| | Indentation consistency | Spaces only (no tabs); consistent indentation width within the same level | | Mapping syntax | Keys followed by `:` with proper spacing | | Sequence syntax | Lines starting with `- ` at proper indentation | | Block scalar indicators | `\|` and `>` followed by optional chomping/indentation indicators | | Flow syntax | Balanced `[]` and `{}` brackets | | Quoted strings | Balanced single and double quotes (handling escape sequences in double-quoted strings) | | Comment syntax | `#` preceded by whitespace or at start of line | | Document markers | `---` and `...` at column 0 only | | Invalid characters | Control characters that are not permitted in YAML | | Anchor/alias syntax | `&name` and `*name` follow valid identifier rules | **Edge case handling:** - Empty string / whitespace-only: returns `{ valid: true, errors: [] }` - Comments-only content: returns `{ valid: true, errors: [] }` - Blank lines: ignored (valid in YAML) **What the validator intentionally does NOT check** (out of scope per requirements): - Schema validation (type correctness, required fields) - YAML stream documents (multiple `---` separated documents beyond basic detection) - Tag resolution (`!!str`, `!!int`, custom tags beyond syntax) - Full YAML 1.2 spec compliance for exotic edge cases ### 3.3 CLI Entry Point (`src/validate-yaml.ts`) Follows the existing `src/index.ts` pattern of reading `process.argv`: ```typescript // Argument parsing const args = process.argv.slice(2); // --help flag or no arguments -> print usage // File path argument -> read file, validate, output result ``` **Output format:** Success: ``` Valid YAML: ``` Error (validation failure): ``` Invalid YAML: Line : Line : ``` Error (file not found): ``` Error: File not found: ``` Error (no arguments): ``` Usage: bun run validate-yaml Validates a YAML file for syntax errors. Options: --help Show this help message Exit codes: 0 YAML is valid 1 YAML is invalid or an error occurred ``` ### 3.4 Data Model No persistent data storage. The validator operates on in-memory string content and returns a result object. No data model changes. ## 4. Technology Stack | Component | Technology | Rationale | |-----------|-----------|-----------| | Runtime | Bun | Existing project runtime | | Language | TypeScript (strict mode) | Existing project language | | File I/O | Bun.file().text() | Bun built-in file API | | CLI args | process.argv | Existing pattern from src/index.ts | | Exit codes | process.exit() | Standard Node.js/Bun API | | Testing | bun:test | Existing project test runner | No new dependencies. No changes to `devDependencies` beyond existing `@types/bun`. ## 5. Implementation Plan | # | Component | Description | Files | |---|-----------|-------------|-------| | T1 | Core YAML Validator | Implement `validateYaml()` function with line-by-line state-tracking parser, types (`ValidationResult`, `ValidationError`), and all validation checks | `src/yaml-validator.ts` | | T2 | CLI Entry Point | Implement command-line interface: argument parsing, file reading, output formatting, exit codes, --help flag | `src/validate-yaml.ts` | | T3 | Unit Tests | Comprehensive tests covering valid YAML, invalid YAML, edge cases (empty, comments-only, whitespace-only), file-not-found, all supported constructs | `src/yaml-validator.test.ts` | | T4 | Script Registration | Add `validate-yaml` script to package.json | `package.json` | ## 6. Implementation DAG **Parallel Groups** (tasks with no inter-dependencies): 1. [T1] - Core validator has no dependencies on other new components 2. [T2, T3, T4] - CLI depends on T1 for import; tests depend on T1 for import; script registration is logically independent but best done after T2 exists **Dependencies**: - T2 -> T1 (interface: CLI imports `validateYaml` from yaml-validator module) - T3 -> T1 (interface: tests import `validateYaml` from yaml-validator module) **Critical Path**: T1 -> T2 ## 7. Testing Strategy ### 7.1 Test Value Assessment | Test Category | Value | Rationale | |---------------|-------|-----------| | Core validation logic (valid YAML accepted) | HIGH | App-specific business logic -- the whole purpose of the feature | | Core validation logic (invalid YAML rejected with correct errors) | HIGH | App-specific error handling -- must produce actionable messages | | Edge cases (empty, whitespace, comments) | HIGH | App requirement FR-004; boundary conditions | | CLI argument handling | MEDIUM | App-specific integration; verifiable via exit codes | | File I/O error handling | MEDIUM | App-specific error path; verifiable via non-existent path | **Tests NOT designed for** (no value): - Testing that Bun.file() reads files correctly (Bun built-in behavior) - Testing that process.exit() sets exit codes (Node.js/Bun runtime behavior) - Testing TypeScript type checking (compiler responsibility) ### 7.2 Test Plan All tests in `src/yaml-validator.test.ts` using `bun:test` with `describe`/`test`/`expect`. **Test Groups:** | Group | Tests | Traces To | |-------|-------|-----------| | Valid YAML - Basic | Simple key-value mapping; nested mapping; sequence; mixed mapping and sequence | FR-006 | | Valid YAML - Advanced | Multi-line strings (literal `\|`, folded `>`); flow sequences `[]`; flow mappings `{}`; quoted strings; inline comments; anchors and aliases | FR-006 | | Valid YAML - Edge Cases | Empty string; whitespace only; comments only; document markers (`---`, `...`) | FR-004 | | Invalid YAML - Syntax Errors | Tab indentation; inconsistent indentation; missing colon in mapping; unbalanced brackets; unbalanced quotes; invalid characters | FR-001 AC-2, FR-002 | | Error Message Quality | Line numbers present and correct; descriptions are human-readable | FR-002 | | Validation Result Structure | `valid` is boolean; `errors` is array; each error has `line` (number) and `message` (string) | FR-002 | ## 8. Deployment Design No deployment infrastructure changes. The command is invoked locally via: ```bash bun run validate-yaml # or directly: bun run src/validate-yaml.ts ``` The new `validate-yaml` script is added to `package.json`: ```json { "scripts": { "validate-yaml": "bun run src/validate-yaml.ts" } } ``` No CI/CD pipeline changes required. # Design Decisions: Simple YAML Validator Command

**Feature ID**: add a simple yaml validator command without adding new deps
**Created**: 2026-04-06

## Decision Log

| ID | Decision | Choice | Rationale | Alternatives Considered |
|----|----------|--------|-----------|------------------------|
| D1 | YAML parsing approach | Line-by-line state-tracking parser | Simplest approach that handles common YAML constructs; aligns with "simple" in feature name; avoids building a full AST when only syntax validation is needed | Recursive descent parser (overkill for syntax-only validation; higher complexity), regex-only approach (too fragile for stateful constructs like block scalars and flow contexts) |
| D2 | File organization | Separate entry point (`src/validate-yaml.ts`) + core module (`src/yaml-validator.ts`) | Follows existing separation pattern (index.ts for entry, utils.ts for logic); keeps validation logic as pure, testable functions decoupled from I/O | Single file combining CLI and logic (less testable, harder to maintain), adding to existing utils.ts (unrelated concern, file would grow too large) |
| D3 | CLI invocation pattern | `bun run validate-yaml <file>` via package.json script | Follows the existing `bun run dev` pattern established in package.json; discoverable through standard npm/bun script listing | Subcommand of existing index.ts (changes existing entry point behavior, couples features), global binary installation (requires build step and bin configuration) |
| D4 | Output format | Plain text with structured error lines | Meets terminal usability requirement (NFR 6.3); simple enough for both human reading and basic programmatic parsing | JSON output (less human-readable for terminal use), ANSI-colored output (would require either a dependency or manual ANSI escape codes, adding complexity) |
| D5 | Error detail level | Line number + human-readable description | Directly satisfies FR-002 acceptance criteria; provides actionable information for developers to locate and fix errors | Column-level precision (significantly more complex to implement with marginal practical value for YAML), stack-trace style output (too verbose, not user-friendly) |
| D6 | Exported API surface | Single `validateYaml(content: string)` function returning `ValidationResult` | Minimal public API surface; pure function with no side effects; easy to test; CLI layer handles all I/O concerns separately | Multiple granular exported functions (unnecessary complexity, breaks encapsulation of parsing state), class-based API (against project's functional style in utils.ts) |

| Test framework | bun:test with describe/test/expect | KB: patterns.md (Testing) | Project's established test runner and pattern |
| File naming | kebab-case (yaml-validator.ts, validate-yaml.ts) | KB: patterns.md (Naming) | Project convention for TypeScript module files |
| Function naming | camelCase (validateYaml) | KB: patterns.md (Naming) | Project convention for functions |
| Type naming | PascalCase (ValidationResult, ValidationError) | KB: patterns.md (Naming) | Project convention for types |
| Test co-location | yaml-validator.test.ts alongside yaml-validator.ts | KB: patterns.md (Testing) | Project convention for test file placement |
| Module system | ESM (import/export) | KB: patterns.md (Code Style), package.json type:module | Project uses ESM modules exclusively |
| Error handling style | try/catch with descriptive messages | KB: patterns.md (Error Handling) | Project convention; no external error libraries |

     5→# Requirements Specification: Simple YAML Validator Command
     6→
     7→**Feature ID**: add a simple yaml validator command without adding new deps

    24→- Provides a self-contained utility that aligns with the project's zero-external-dependency philosophy.

    29→
    30→| Metric | Target |
    31→|--------|--------|
    32→| Valid YAML correctly identified | 100% of well-formed YAML inputs are reported as valid |
    33→| Invalid YAML correctly identified | 100% of malformed YAML inputs are reported as invalid with a meaningful error description |
    34→| No new dependencies added | `package.json` dependencies and devDependencies remain unchanged (except `@types/bun`) |
    35→| Command execution time | Completes validation of a typical config file (under 1000 lines) in under 1 second |
    36→

    38→
    39→### 3.1 User Types
    40→
    41→| User Type | Description | Interaction |
    42→|-----------|-------------|-------------|
    43→| Developer | A developer using the project's CLI tools to validate YAML configuration files | Invokes the validator command from the terminal, passing a file path or piped input |
    44→| CI/CD Pipeline | An automated process that needs to gate deployments on configuration correctness | Invokes the validator command and relies on the exit code to determine pass/fail |
    45→
    46→### 3.2 Stakeholder Interests
    47→
    48→| Stakeholder | Interest |
    49→|-------------|----------|
    50→| Project Maintainers | Keep the project dependency-free; ensure new commands follow existing code patterns |
    51→| End Users | Receive clear, actionable feedback about YAML validity without installing extra tools |

    55→### 4.1 In Scope
    56→
    57→- A command that can be invoked to validate a YAML file provided as a file path argument.

    59→- Appropriate exit codes: zero for valid YAML, non-zero for invalid YAML or errors.
    60→- Support for standard YAML syntax (mappings, sequences, scalars, multi-line strings, comments, anchors/aliases).
    61→- Unit tests covering valid YAML, invalid YAML, edge cases (empty input, non-existent file).
    62→
    63→### 4.2 Out of Scope
    64→
    65→- YAML schema validation (validating against a specific schema or structure beyond syntax).
    66→- YAML linting or style enforcement (indentation preferences, key ordering, etc.).
    67→- YAML transformation, formatting, or pretty-printing.
    68→- Support for YAML stream documents (multiple documents separated by `---`) beyond basic detection.
    69→- Interactive or GUI-based validation.
    70→- Adding any new runtime or development dependencies to the project.

    79→
    80→### FR-001: Validate YAML File from File Path
    81→**Priority**: Must Have
    82→**User Type**: Developer, CI/CD Pipeline
    83→**Requirement**: A user must be able to invoke the validator by providing a file path as a command-line argument. The system reads the file and reports whether its contents are valid YAML.

    88→- AC-3: Given a non-existent file path, the command outputs a clear error message stating the file was not found.
    89→
    90→### FR-002: Provide Meaningful Error Messages
    91→**Priority**: Must Have
    92→**User Type**: Developer
    93→**Requirement**: When YAML is invalid, the validator must report the approximate location (line number) of the error and a human-readable description of the problem.
    94→**Rationale**: Developers need actionable feedback to fix YAML errors efficiently; a simple "invalid" message is not sufficient.
    95→**Acceptance Criteria**:
    96→- AC-1: Error output includes the line number where the problem was detected.
    97→- AC-2: Error output includes a description of what was expected vs. what was found (e.g., "unexpected indentation", "invalid character").
    98→
    99→### FR-003: Return Appropriate Exit Codes
   100→**Priority**: Must Have
   101→**User Type**: CI/CD Pipeline
   102→**Requirement**: The command must return exit code 0 when the input YAML is valid, and a non-zero exit code when the input is invalid or an error occurs.
   103→**Rationale**: Automated pipelines rely on exit codes to determine success or failure without parsing output text.
   104→**Acceptance Criteria**:
   105→- AC-1: Exit code is 0 when the provided YAML is syntactically valid.
   106→- AC-2: Exit code is 1 (or another non-zero value) when the provided YAML is syntactically invalid.
   107→- AC-3: Exit code is non-zero when an operational error occurs (e.g., file not found, permission denied).
   108→

   110→**Priority**: Should Have
   111→**User Type**: Developer
   112→**Requirement**: The validator should handle edge cases such as empty files, files containing only comments, and files containing only whitespace without crashing or producing misleading results.

   114→**Acceptance Criteria**:
   115→- AC-1: An empty file is treated as valid YAML (an empty document is valid per the YAML specification).
   116→- AC-2: A file containing only YAML comments is treated as valid YAML.
   117→- AC-3: A file containing only whitespace is treated as valid YAML.
   118→- AC-4: The command does not crash or produce a stack trace for any of these edge cases.

   130→**Priority**: Should Have
   131→**User Type**: Developer
   132→**Requirement**: The validator should correctly identify the validity of common YAML constructs including key-value mappings, sequences (lists), nested structures, quoted strings, multi-line strings (literal and folded block scalars), and comments.

   156→- The command must provide a `--help` flag (or equivalent) that describes usage.
   157→- Error messages must be written in plain language, not raw parser internals.
   158→- Output should be suitable for terminal display (no excessive verbosity for valid files).
   159→

   161→
   162→- No additional compliance requirements beyond the zero-dependency constraint.

   164→## 7. User Stories

   167→**As a** developer

# Development Tasks: Simple YAML Validator Command

**Feature ID**: add a simple yaml validator command without adding new deps
**Status**: Not Started
**Progress**: 0% (0 of 7 tasks)
**Estimated Effort**: 2.5 days
**Started**: 2026-04-06

## Overview

Implement a lightweight, zero-dependency YAML syntax validator as a CLI command. The validator reads a YAML file by path, checks contents for syntactic correctness using a custom line-by-line state-tracking parser, and reports clear success or failure with actionable error messages and appropriate exit codes. Three new files are added (`src/yaml-validator.ts`, `src/validate-yaml.ts`, `src/yaml-validator.test.ts`) plus a script entry in `package.json`.

## Implementation DAG

**Parallel Groups** (tasks with no inter-dependencies):

1. [T1] - Core validator has no dependencies on other new components
2. [T2, T3, T4] - CLI depends on T1 for import; tests depend on T1 for import; script registration is logically independent but best done after T2 exists

**Dependencies**:

- T2 -> T1 (interface: CLI imports `validateYaml` from yaml-validator module)
- T3 -> T1 (interface: tests import `validateYaml` from yaml-validator module)

**Critical Path**: T1 -> T2

## Task Subflow

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> T1
    T1 : T1 Core YAML Validator
    T1 --> T2
    T2 : T2 CLI Entry Point
    T1 --> T3
    T3 : T3 Unit Tests
    T1 --> T4
    T4 : T4 Script Registration
    T2 --> TD1
    T3 --> TD2
    T4 --> TD3
    TD1 : TD1 Update index.md
    TD2 : TD2 Update architecture.md
    TD3 : TD3 Update modules.md
    TD1 --> [*]
    TD2 --> [*]
    TD3 --> [*]
```

## Task Breakdown

### Foundation

- [ ] **T1**: Implement core YAML validator module with `validateYaml()` function, `ValidationResult` and `ValidationError` types, and line-by-line state-tracking parser covering indentation consistency, mapping/sequence syntax, block scalars, flow syntax, quoted strings, comment syntax, document markers, invalid characters, and anchor/alias validation `[complexity:complex]`

    **Reference**: [design.md#3-detailed-design](design.md#3-detailed-design)

    **Effort**: 8 hours

    **Acceptance Criteria**:

    - [ ] `src/yaml-validator.ts` exports `validateYaml(content: string): ValidationResult`
    - [ ] `ValidationResult` contains `valid: boolean` and `errors: ValidationError[]`
    - [ ] `ValidationError` contains `line: number` and `message: string`
    - [ ] Validates indentation consistency (spaces only, no tabs, consistent width)
    - [ ] Validates mapping syntax (keys followed by `:` with proper spacing)
    - [ ] Validates sequence syntax (lines starting with `- ` at proper indentation)
    - [ ] Validates block scalar indicators (`|` and `>` with optional modifiers)
    - [ ] Validates flow syntax (balanced `[]` and `{}` brackets)
    - [ ] Validates quoted strings (balanced single and double quotes, escape handling)
    - [ ] Validates comment syntax (`#` preceded by whitespace or at start of line)
    - [ ] Validates document markers (`---` and `...` at column 0 only)
    - [ ] Detects invalid control characters
    - [ ] Validates anchor (`&name`) and alias (`*name`) syntax
    - [ ] Empty string, whitespace-only, and comments-only input returns `{ valid: true, errors: [] }`

### CLI and Integration

- [ ] **T2**: Implement CLI entry point with argument parsing (`process.argv`), file reading (`Bun.file().text()`), output formatting (success/error messages per design spec), exit codes (0 for valid, 1 for invalid/error), and `--help` flag support `[complexity:medium]`

    **Reference**: [design.md#33-cli-entry-point](design.md#33-cli-entry-point)

    **Effort**: 4 hours

    **Acceptance Criteria**:

    - [ ] `src/validate-yaml.ts` reads file path from `process.argv`
    - [ ] Running with `--help` or no arguments prints usage information and exits

The new file `/private/tmp/rp1-evals/9ebc041b/workspace/src/yaml-validator.ts` exports:

- **`ValidationError`** interface: `{ line: number; message: string }`
- **`ValidationResult`** interface: `{ valid: boolean; errors: ValidationError[] }`
- **`validateYaml(content: string): ValidationResult`** -- the primary validation function

The validator uses a line-by-line state-tracking parser with three key components:

1. **`validateYaml`** -- Main orchestrator maintaining parser state across lines:
   - Block scalar mode (tracks `|` and `>` block content by indentation)
   - Flow context (bracket stack for `[]` and `{}` nesting)
   - Multi-line quoted strings (tracks open quotes across line boundaries)
   - Indentation stack (validates dedent matches a known level)
   - Anchor/alias tracking (validates aliases reference defined anchors)

2. **`scanLine`** -- Character-by-character line scanner that handles:
   - Double-quoted strings with escape sequences (`\"`, `\\`)
   - Single-quoted strings with escaped single quotes (`''`)
   - Flow bracket open/close with stack validation
   - Anchor (`&name`) and alias (`*name`) detection
   - Block scalar indicator detection (`|`, `>` with optional modifiers)
   - Comment boundaries (`#` preceded by whitespace)

3. **`checkControlCharacters`** -- Validates no invalid control characters (codes below 0x09, between 0x0e-0x1f, or 0x7f)

Edge cases handled: empty content, whitespace-only, comments-only, document markers (`---`, `...`), and all return `{ valid: true, errors: [] }` as appropriate.

     4→---
     5→# Requirements Specification: Simple YAML Validator Command
     6→
     7→**Feature ID**: add a simple yaml validator command without adding new deps
     8→**Version**: 1.0.0
     9→**Status**: Draft
    10→**Created**: 2026-04-06
    11→
    12→## 1. Feature Overview
    13→
    14→The project needs a command-line capability that accepts a YAML file (or YAML input) and validates whether it conforms to valid YAML syntax. This validator must be implemented using only the project's existing dependencies (Bun built-ins and TypeScript) -- no new packages or external libraries may be introduced. The command should provide clear, actionable feedback to users about whether their YAML is valid and, if not, where the problem lies.
    15→
    16→## 2. Business Context
    17→
    18→### 2.1 Problem Statement
    19→
    20→Users of the rp1-eval-project currently have no built-in way to check whether a YAML file is syntactically correct. YAML is a common configuration format, and syntax errors in YAML files can cause downstream failures that are difficult to diagnose. A lightweight, zero-dependency validation command would allow users to catch YAML errors early without installing additional tooling.
    21→
    22→### 2.2 Business Value
    23→
    24→- Provides a self-contained utility that aligns with the project's zero-external-dependency philosophy.
    25→- Reduces friction for users working with YAML configuration files by offering quick, local validation.
    26→- Extends the project's utility module with a practical, reusable capability.
    27→
    28→### 2.3 Success Metrics
    29→
    30→| Metric | Target |
    31→|--------|--------|
    32→| Valid YAML correctly identified | 100% of well-formed YAML inputs are reported as valid |
    33→| Invalid YAML correctly identified | 100% of malformed YAML inputs are reported as invalid with a meaningful error description |
    34→| No new dependencies added | `package.json` dependencies and devDependencies remain unchanged (except `@types/bun`) |
    35→| Command execution time | Completes validation of a typical config file (under 1000 lines) in under 1 second |
    36→
    37→## 3. Stakeholders & Users
    38→
    39→### 3.1 User Types
    40→
    41→| User Type | Description | Interaction |
    42→|-----------|-------------|-------------|
    43→| Developer | A developer using the project's CLI tools to validate YAML configuration files | Invokes the validator command from the terminal, passing a file path or piped input |
    44→| CI/CD Pipeline | An automated process that needs to gate deployments on configuration correctness | Invokes the validator command and relies on the exit code to determine pass/fail |
    45→
    46→### 3.2 Stakeholder Interests
    47→
    48→| Stakeholder | Interest |
    49→|-------------|----------|
    50→| Project Maintainers | Keep the project dependency-free; ensure new commands follow existing code patterns |
    51→| End Users | Receive clear, actionable feedback about YAML validity without installing extra tools |
    52→
    53→## 4. Scope Definition
    54→
    55→### 4.1 In Scope
    56→
    57→- A command that can be invoked to validate a YAML file provided as a file path argument.
    58→- Reporting of validation results: valid or invalid with error details (line number, description of the problem).
    59→- Appropriate exit codes: zero for valid YAML, non-zero for invalid YAML or errors.
    60→- Support for standard YAML syntax (mappings, sequences, scalars, multi-line strings, comments, anchors/aliases).
    61→- Unit tests covering valid YAML, invalid YAML, edge cases (empty input, non-existent file).
    62→
    63→### 4.2 Out of Scope
    64→
    65→- YAML schema validation (validating against a specific schema or structure beyond syntax).
    66→- YAML linting or style enforcement (indentation preferences, key ordering, etc.).
    67→- YAML transformation, formatting, or pretty-printing.
    68→- Support for YAML stream documents (multiple documents separated by `---`) beyond basic detection.
    69→- Interactive or GUI-based validation.
    70→- Adding any new runtime or development dependencies to the project.
    71→
    72→### 4.3 Assumptions
    73→
    74→- Bun's runtime environment provides sufficient built-in capabilities (file I/O, string processing) to implement a basic YAML syntax validator without external libraries.
    75→- The validator targets YAML 1.2 core schema syntax at a practical level; exhaustive compliance with every edge case of the YAML 1.2 specification is not required for an MVP.
    76→- Users will provide input as a file path argument to the command.
    77→
    78→## 5. Functional Requirements
    79→
    80→### FR-001: Validate YAML File from File Path
    81→**Priority**: Must Have
    82→**User Type**: Developer, CI/CD Pipeline
    83→**Requirement**: A user must be able to invoke the validator by providing a file path as a command-line argument. The system reads the file and reports whether its contents are valid YAML.
    84→**Rationale**: File-based validation is the primary use case for checking configuration files.
    85→**Acceptance Criteria**:
    86→- AC-1: Given a valid YAML file path, the command outputs a success message indicating the file is valid.
    87→- AC-2: Given an invalid YAML file path (malformed YAML), the command outputs an error message describing the syntax problem.
    88→- AC-3: Given a non-existent file path, the command outputs a clear error message stating the file was not found.
    89→
    90→### FR-002: Provide Meaningful Error Messages
    91→**Priority**: Must Have
    92→**User Type**: Developer
    93→**Requirement**: When YAML is invalid, the validator must report the approximate location (line number) of the error and a human-readable description of the problem.
    94→**Rationale**: Developers need actionable feedback to fix YAML errors efficiently; a simple "invalid" message is not sufficient.
    95→**Acceptance Criteria**:
    96→- AC-1: Error output includes the line number where the problem was detected.
    97→- AC-2: Error output includes a description of what was expected vs. what was found (e.g., "unexpected indentation", "invalid character").
    98→
    99→### FR-003: Return Appropriate Exit Codes
   100→**Priority**: Must Have
   101→**User Type**: CI/CD Pipeline
   102→**Requirement**: The command must return exit code 0 when the input YAML is valid, and a non-zero exit code when the input is invalid or an error occurs.
   103→**Rationale**: Automated pipelines rely on exit codes to determine success or failure without parsing output text.
   104→**Acceptance Criteria**:
   105→- AC-1: Exit code is 0 when the provided YAML is syntactically valid.
   106→- AC-2: Exit code is 1 (or another non-zero value) when the provided YAML is syntactically invalid.
   107→- AC-3: Exit code is non-zero when an operational error occurs (e.g., file not found, permission denied).
   108→
   109→### FR-004: Handle Edge Cases Gracefully
   110→**Priority**: Should Have
   111→**User Type**: Developer
   112→**Requirement**: The validator should handle edge cases such as empty files, files containing only comments, and files containing only whitespace without crashing or producing misleading results.
   113→**Rationale**: Real-world YAML files may be empty or contain only comments; the validator should not report these as errors.
   114→**Acceptance Criteria**:
   115→- AC-1: An empty file is treated as valid YAML (an empty document is valid per the YAML specification).
   116→- AC-2: A file containing only YAML comments is treated as valid YAML.
   117→- AC-3: A file containing only whitespace is treated as valid YAML.
   118→- AC-4: The command does not crash or produce a stack trace for any of these edge cases.
   119→
   120→### FR-005: No New Dependencies
   121→**Priority**: Must Have
   122→**User Type**: Project Maintainers
   123→**Requirement**: The validator must be implemented using only the existing project dependencies (Bun built-ins, TypeScript). No new entries may be added to `dependencies` or `devDependencies` in `package.json`.
   124→**Rationale**: The project follows a zero-external-dependency philosophy. The feature request explicitly states "without adding new deps."
   125→**Acceptance Criteria**:
   126→- AC-1: The `package.json` file has no new entries in `dependencies` or `devDependencies` after the feature is implemented.
   127→- AC-2: No `node_modules` additions beyond what already exists.
   128→
   129→### FR-006: Validate Common YAML Constructs
   130→**Priority**: Should Have
   131→**User Type**: Developer
   132→**Requirement**: The validator should correctly identify the validity of common YAML constructs including key-value mappings, sequences (lists), nested structures, quoted strings, multi-line strings (literal and folded block scalars), and comments.
   133→**Rationale**: These are the most frequently used YAML features in configuration files, and the validator must handle them to be practically useful.
   134→**Acceptance Criteria**:
   135→- AC-1: A file with nested key-value mappings is correctly validated.
   136→- AC-2: A file with sequences (both block and flow style) is correctly validated.
   137→- AC-3: A file with multi-line strings (using `|` or `>`) is correctly validated.
   138→- AC-4: A file with inline comments is correctly validated.
   139→
   140→## 6. Non-Functional Requirements
   141→
   142→### 6.1 Performance Expectations
   143→
   144→| Expectation | Target |
   145→|-------------|--------|
   146→| Validation of a file under 1000 lines | Completes in under 1 second |
   147→| Validation of a file under 100 lines | Completes in under 200 milliseconds |
   148→
   149→### 6.2 Security Requirements
   150→
   151→- The command must only read the file specified; it must not write to, modify, or delete any files.
   152→- The command must not execute or evaluate any content within the YAML file.
   153→
   154→### 6.3 Usability Requirements
   155→
   156→- The command must provide a `--help` flag (or equivalent) that describes usage.
   157→- Error messages must be written in plain language, not raw parser internals.
   158→- Output should be suitable for terminal display (no excessive verbosity for valid files).
   159→
   160→### 6.4 Compliance Requirements
   161→
   162→- No additional compliance requirements beyond the zero-dependency constraint.
   163→
   164→## 7. User Stories
   165→
   166→### STORY-001: Validate a Configuration File
   167→**As a** developer
   168→**I want to** run a command that checks my YAML configuration file for syntax errors
   169→**So that** I can catch mistakes before they cause failures in my application or deployment pipeline.
   170→
   171→**Acceptance Scenarios**:
   172→- GIVEN a YAML file with correct syntax, WHEN I run the validator command with the file path, THEN I see a message confirming the file is valid and the process exits with code 0.
   173→- GIVEN a YAML file with a missing colon after a key, WHEN I run the validator command with the file path, THEN I see an error message indicating the line and nature of the problem and the process exits with a non-zero code.
   174→
   175→### STORY-002: Gate a CI Pipeline on YAML Validity
   176→**As a** CI/CD pipeline
   177→**I want to** invoke the YAML validator and use its exit code to determine if configuration files are correct
   178→**So that** deployments are blocked when configuration files contain syntax errors.
   179→
   180→**Acceptance Scenarios**:
   181→- GIVEN a valid YAML configuration file, WHEN the validator is invoked in a pipeline step, THEN the step succeeds (exit code 0).
   182→- GIVEN an invalid YAML configuration file, WHEN the validator is invoked in a pipeline step, THEN the step fails (non-zero exit code) and the error details are visible in the pipeline log.
   183→
   184→### STORY-003: Get Help on Command Usage
   185→**As a** developer unfamiliar with the tool
   186→**I want to** see usage instructions when I pass a help flag
   187→**So that** I understand how to invoke the validator correctly.
   188→
   189→**Acceptance Scenarios**:
   190→- GIVEN no file argument or a `--help` flag, WHEN I run the validator command, THEN I see a usage message describing how to provide a file path.
   191→
   192→## 8. Business Rules
   193→
   194→| Rule ID | Rule | Rationale |
   195→|---------|------|-----------|
   196→| BR-001 | The project must not gain any new runtime or development dependencies | Aligns with the project's zero-dependency philosophy and the explicit feature constraint |
   197→| BR-002 | The validator only checks syntax, not semantic correctness | Keeps scope focused and implementation feasible without external schema libraries |
   198→| BR-003 | Empty YAML documents are considered valid | Per the YAML specification, an empty document is a valid YAML document |
   199→
   200→## 9. Dependencies & Constraints
   201→
   202→| Dependency / Constraint | Type | Impact |
   203→|-------------------------|------|--------|
   204→| Bun runtime | Platform | The command runs under Bun; must use Bun-compatible APIs for file I/O and process management |
   205→| No external YAML parsing library | Constraint | The YAML validation logic must be implemented from scratch or using only built-in capabilities |
   206→| Existing project patterns | Constraint | New code must follow established naming conventions (camelCase functions, kebab-case files, PascalCase types), testing patterns (co-located `*.test.ts`), and error handling style (try/catch with descriptive messages) |
   207→

   209→
   210→| # | Question | Resolution | Source |
   211→|---|----------|------------|--------|
   212→| 1 | What YAML specification version should be targeted? | YAML 1.2 core schema at a practical level; exhaustive compliance not required for MVP | Inferred -- industry standard |

     5→# Requirements Specification: Simple YAML Validator Command
     6→
     7→**Feature ID**: add a simple yaml validator command without adding new deps
     8→**Version**: 1.0.0
     9→**Status**: Draft
    10→**Created**: 2026-04-06
    11→
    12→## 1. Feature Overview
    13→
    14→The project needs a command-line capability that accepts a YAML file (or YAML input) and validates whether it conforms to valid YAML syntax. This validator must be implemented using only the project's existing dependencies (Bun built-ins and TypeScript) -- no new packages or external libraries may be introduced. The command should provide clear, actionable feedback to users about whether their YAML is valid and, if not, where the problem lies.
    15→
    16→## 2. Business Context
    17→
    18→### 2.1 Problem Statement
    19→
    20→Users of the rp1-eval-project currently have no built-in way to check whether a YAML file is syntactically correct. YAML is a common configuration format, and syntax errors in YAML files can cause downstream failures that are difficult to diagnose. A lightweight, zero-dependency validation command would allow users to catch YAML errors early without installing additional tooling.
    21→
    22→### 2.2 Business Value
    23→
    24→- Provides a self-contained utility that aligns with the project's zero-external-dependency philosophy.
    25→- Reduces friction for users working with YAML configuration files by offering quick, local validation.
    26→- Extends the project's utility module with a practical, reusable capability.
    27→
    28→### 2.3 Success Metrics
    29→
    30→| Metric | Target |
    31→|--------|--------|
    32→| Valid YAML correctly identified | 100% of well-formed YAML inputs are reported as valid |
    33→| Invalid YAML correctly identified | 100% of malformed YAML inputs are reported as invalid with a meaningful error description |
    34→| No new dependencies added | `package.json` dependencies and devDependencies remain unchanged (except `@types/bun`) |
    35→| Command execution time | Completes validation of a typical config file (under 1000 lines) in under 1 second |
    36→
    37→## 3. Stakeholders & Users
    38→
    39→### 3.1 User Types
    40→
    41→| User Type | Description | Interaction |
    42→|-----------|-------------|-------------|
    43→| Developer | A developer using the project's CLI tools to validate YAML configuration files | Invokes the validator command from the terminal, passing a file path or piped input |
    44→| CI/CD Pipeline | An automated process that needs to gate deployments on configuration correctness | Invokes the validator command and relies on the exit code to determine pass/fail |
    45→
    46→### 3.2 Stakeholder Interests
    47→
    48→| Stakeholder | Interest |
    49→|-------------|----------|
    50→| Project Maintainers | Keep the project dependency-free; ensure new commands follow existing code patterns |
    51→| End Users | Receive clear, actionable feedback about YAML validity without installing extra tools |
    52→
    53→## 4. Scope Definition
    54→
    55→### 4.1 In Scope
    56→
    57→- A command that can be invoked to validate a YAML file provided as a file path argument.
    58→- Reporting of validation results: valid or invalid with error details (line number, description of the problem).
    59→- Appropriate exit codes: zero for valid YAML, non-zero for invalid YAML or errors.
    60→- Support for standard YAML syntax (mappings, sequences, scalars, multi-line strings, comments, anchors/aliases).
    61→- Unit tests covering valid YAML, invalid YAML, edge cases (empty input, non-existent file).
    62→
    63→### 4.2 Out of Scope
    64→
    65→- YAML schema validation (validating against a specific schema or structure beyond syntax).
    66→- YAML linting or style enforcement (indentation preferences, key ordering, etc.).
    67→- YAML transformation, formatting, or pretty-printing.
    68→- Support for YAML stream documents (multiple documents separated by `---`) beyond basic detection.
    69→- Interactive or GUI-based validation.
    70→- Adding any new runtime or development dependencies to the project.
    71→
    72→### 4.3 Assumptions
    73→
    74→- Bun's runtime environment provides sufficient built-in capabilities (file I/O, string processing) to implement a basic YAML syntax validator without external libraries.
    75→- The validator targets YAML 1.2 core schema syntax at a practical level; exhaustive compliance with every edge case of the YAML 1.2 specification is not required for an MVP.
    76→- Users will provide input as a file path argument to the command.
    77→
    78→## 5. Functional Requirements
    79→
    80→### FR-001: Validate YAML File from File Path
    81→**Priority**: Must Have
    82→**User Type**: Developer, CI/CD Pipeline
    83→**Requirement**: A user must be able to invoke the validator by providing a file path as a command-line argument. The system reads the file and reports whether its contents are valid YAML.
    84→**Rationale**: File-based validation is the primary use case for checking configuration files.
    85→**Acceptance Criteria**:
    86→- AC-1: Given a valid YAML file path, the command outputs a success message indicating the file is valid.
    87→- AC-2: Given an invalid YAML file path (malformed YAML), the command outputs an error message describing the syntax problem.
    88→- AC-3: Given a non-existent file path, the command outputs a clear error message stating the file was not found.
    89→
    90→### FR-002: Provide Meaningful Error Messages
    91→**Priority**: Must Have
    92→**User Type**: Developer
    93→**Requirement**: When YAML is invalid, the validator must report the approximate location (line number) of the error and a human-readable description of the problem.
    94→**Rationale**: Developers need actionable feedback to fix YAML errors efficiently; a simple "invalid" message is not sufficient.
    95→**Acceptance Criteria**:
    96→- AC-1: Error output includes the line number where the problem was detected.
    97→- AC-2: Error output includes a description of what was expected vs. what was found (e.g., "unexpected indentation", "invalid character").
    98→
    99→### FR-003: Return Appropriate Exit Codes
   100→**Priority**: Must Have
   101→**User Type**: CI/CD Pipeline
   102→**Requirement**: The command must return exit code 0 when the input YAML is valid, and a non-zero exit code when the input is invalid or an error occurs.
   103→**Rationale**: Automated pipelines rely on exit codes to determine success or failure without parsing output text.
   104→**Acceptance Criteria**:
   105→- AC-1: Exit code is 0 when the provided YAML is syntactically valid.
   106→- AC-2: Exit code is 1 (or another non-zero value) when the provided YAML is syntactically invalid.
   107→- AC-3: Exit code is non-zero when an operational error occurs (e.g., file not found, permission denied).
   108→
   109→### FR-004: Handle Edge Cases Gracefully
   110→**Priority**: Should Have
   111→**User Type**: Developer
   112→**Requirement**: The validator should handle edge cases such as empty files, files containing only comments, and files containing only whitespace without crashing or producing misleading results.
   113→**Rationale**: Real-world YAML files may be empty or contain only comments; the validator should not report these as errors.
   114→**Acceptance Criteria**:
   115→- AC-1: An empty file is treated as valid YAML (an empty document is valid per the YAML specification).
   116→- AC-2: A file containing only YAML comments is treated as valid YAML.
   117→- AC-3: A file containing only whitespace is treated as valid YAML.
   118→- AC-4: The command does not crash or produce a stack trace for any of these edge cases.
   119→
   120→### FR-005: No New Dependencies
   121→**Priority**: Must Have
   122→**User Type**: Project Maintainers
   123→**Requirement**: The validator must be implemented using only the existing project dependencies (Bun built-ins, TypeScript). No new entries may be added to `dependencies` or `devDependencies` in `package.json`.
   124→**Rationale**: The project follows a zero-external-dependency philosophy. The feature request explicitly states "without adding new deps."
   125→**Acceptance Criteria**:
   126→- AC-1: The `package.json` file has no new entries in `dependencies` or `devDependencies` after the feature is implemented.
   127→- AC-2: No `node_modules` additions beyond what already exists.
   128→
   129→### FR-006: Validate Common YAML Constructs
   130→**Priority**: Should Have
   131→**User Type**: Developer
   132→**Requirement**: The validator should correctly identify the validity of common YAML constructs including key-value mappings, sequences (lists), nested structures, quoted strings, multi-line strings (literal and folded block scalars), and comments.
   133→**Rationale**: These are the most frequently used YAML features in configuration files, and the validator must handle them to be practically useful.
   134→**Acceptance Criteria**:
   135→- AC-1: A file with nested key-value mappings is correctly validated.
   136→- AC-2: A file with sequences (both block and flow style) is correctly validated.
   137→- AC-3: A file with multi-line strings (using `|` or `>`) is correctly validated.
   138→- AC-4: A file with inline comments is correctly validated.
   139→
   140→## 6. Non-Functional Requirements
   141→
   142→### 6.1 Performance Expectations
   143→
   144→| Expectation | Target |
   145→|-------------|--------|
   146→| Validation of a file under 1000 lines | Completes in under 1 second |
   147→| Validation of a file under 100 lines | Completes in under 200 milliseconds |
   148→
   149→### 6.2 Security Requirements
   150→
   151→- The command must only read the file specified; it must not write to, modify, or delete any files.
   152→- The command must not execute or evaluate any content within the YAML file.
   153→
   154→### 6.3 Usability Requirements
   155→
   156→- The command must provide a `--help` flag (or equivalent) that describes usage.
   157→- Error messages must be written in plain language, not raw parser internals.
   158→- Output should be suitable for terminal display (no excessive verbosity for valid files).
   159→
   160→### 6.4 Compliance Requirements
   161→
   162→- No additional compliance requirements beyond the zero-dependency constraint.
   163→
   164→## 7. User Stories
   165→
   166→### STORY-001: Validate a Configuration File
   167→**As a** developer
   168→**I want to** run a command that checks my YAML configuration file for syntax errors

     4→---
     5→# Requirements Specification: Simple YAML Validator Command
     6→
     7→**Feature ID**: add a simple yaml validator command without adding new deps
     8→**Version**: 1.0.0
     9→**Status**: Draft
    10→**Created**: 2026-04-06
    11→
    12→## 1. Feature Overview
    13→
    14→The project needs a command-line capability that accepts a YAML file (or YAML input) and validates whether it conforms to valid YAML syntax. This validator must be implemented using only the project's existing dependencies (Bun built-ins and TypeScript) -- no new packages or external libraries may be introduced. The command should provide clear, actionable feedback to users about whether their YAML is valid and, if not, where the problem lies.
    15→
    16→## 2. Business Context
    17→
    18→### 2.1 Problem Statement
    19→
    20→Users of the rp1-eval-project currently have no built-in way to check whether a YAML file is syntactically correct. YAML is a common configuration format, and syntax errors in YAML files can cause downstream failures that are difficult to diagnose. A lightweight, zero-dependency validation command would allow users to catch YAML errors early without installing additional tooling.
    21→
    22→### 2.2 Business Value
    23→
    24→- Provides a self-contained utility that aligns with the project's zero-external-dependency philosophy.
    25→- Reduces friction for users working with YAML configuration files by offering quick, local validation.
    26→- Extends the project's utility module with a practical, reusable capability.
    27→
    28→### 2.3 Success Metrics
    29→
    30→| Metric | Target |
    31→|--------|--------|
    32→| Valid YAML correctly identified | 100% of well-formed YAML inputs are reported as valid |
    33→| Invalid YAML correctly identified | 100% of malformed YAML inputs are reported as invalid with a meaningful error description |
    34→| No new dependencies added | `package.json` dependencies and devDependencies remain unchanged (except `@types/bun`) |
    35→| Command execution time | Completes validation of a typical config file (under 1000 lines) in under 1 second |
    36→
    37→## 3. Stakeholders & Users
    38→
    39→### 3.1 User Types
    40→
    41→| User Type | Description | Interaction |
    42→|-----------|-------------|-------------|
    43→| Developer | A developer using the project's CLI tools to validate YAML configuration files | Invokes the validator command from the terminal, passing a file path or piped input |
    44→| CI/CD Pipeline | An automated process that needs to gate deployments on configuration correctness | Invokes the validator command and relies on the exit code to determine pass/fail |
    45→
    46→### 3.2 Stakeholder Interests
    47→
    48→| Stakeholder | Interest |
    49→|-------------|----------|
    50→| Project Maintainers | Keep the project dependency-free; ensure new commands follow existing code patterns |
    51→| End Users | Receive clear, actionable feedback about YAML validity without installing extra tools |
    52→
    53→## 4. Scope Definition
    54→
    55→### 4.1 In Scope
    56→
    57→- A command that can be invoked to validate a YAML file provided as a file path argument.
    58→- Reporting of validation results: valid or invalid with error details (line number, description of the problem).
    59→- Appropriate exit codes: zero for valid YAML, non-zero for invalid YAML or errors.
    60→- Support for standard YAML syntax (mappings, sequences, scalars, multi-line strings, comments, anchors/aliases).
    61→- Unit tests covering valid YAML, invalid YAML, edge cases (empty input, non-existent file).
    62→
    63→### 4.2 Out of Scope
    64→
    65→- YAML schema validation (validating against a specific schema or structure beyond syntax).
    66→- YAML linting or style enforcement (indentation preferences, key ordering, etc.).
    67→- YAML transformation, formatting, or pretty-printing.
    68→- Support for YAML stream documents (multiple documents separated by `---`) beyond basic detection.
    69→- Interactive or GUI-based validation.
    70→- Adding any new runtime or development dependencies to the project.
    71→
    72→### 4.3 Assumptions
    73→
    74→- Bun's runtime environment provides sufficient built-in capabilities (file I/O, string processing) to implement a basic YAML syntax validator without external libraries.
    75→- The validator targets YAML 1.2 core schema syntax at a practical level; exhaustive compliance with every edge case of the YAML 1.2 specification is not required for an MVP.
    76→- Users will provide input as a file path argument to the command.
    77→
    78→## 5. Functional Requirements
    79→
    80→### FR-001: Validate YAML File from File Path
    81→**Priority**: Must Have
    82→**User Type**: Developer, CI/CD Pipeline
    83→**Requirement**: A user must be able to invoke the validator by providing a file path as a command-line argument. The system reads the file and reports whether its contents are valid YAML.
    84→**Rationale**: File-based validation is the primary use case for checking configuration files.
    85→**Acceptance Criteria**:
    86→- AC-1: Given a valid YAML file path, the command outputs a success message indicating the file is valid.
    87→- AC-2: Given an invalid YAML file path (malformed YAML), the command outputs an error message describing the syntax problem.
    88→- AC-3: Given a non-existent file path, the command outputs a clear error message stating the file was not found.
    89→
    90→### FR-002: Provide Meaningful Error Messages
    91→**Priority**: Must Have
    92→**User Type**: Developer
    93→**Requirement**: When YAML is invalid, the validator must report the approximate location (line number) of the error and a human-readable description of the problem.
    94→**Rationale**: Developers need actionable feedback to fix YAML errors efficiently; a simple "invalid" message is not sufficient.
    95→**Acceptance Criteria**:
    96→- AC-1: Error output includes the line number where the problem was detected.
    97→- AC-2: Error output includes a description of what was expected vs. what was found (e.g., "unexpected indentation", "invalid character").
    98→
    99→### FR-003: Return Appropriate Exit Codes
   100→**Priority**: Must Have
   101→**User Type**: CI/CD Pipeline
   102→**Requirement**: The command must return exit code 0 when the input YAML is valid, and a non-zero exit code when the input is invalid or an error occurs.
   103→**Rationale**: Automated pipelines rely on exit codes to determine success or failure without parsing output text.
   104→**Acceptance Criteria**:
   105→- AC-1: Exit code is 0 when the provided YAML is syntactically valid.
   106→- AC-2: Exit code is 1 (or another non-zero value) when the provided YAML is syntactically invalid.
   107→- AC-3: Exit code is non-zero when an operational error occurs (e.g., file not found, permission denied).
   108→
   109→### FR-004: Handle Edge Cases Gracefully
   110→**Priority**: Should Have
   111→**User Type**: Developer
   112→**Requirement**: The validator should handle edge cases such as empty files, files containing only comments, and files containing only whitespace without crashing or producing misleading results.
   113→**Rationale**: Real-world YAML files may be empty or contain only comments; the validator should not report these as errors.
   114→**Acceptance Criteria**:
   115→- AC-1: An empty file is treated as valid YAML (an empty document is valid per the YAML specification).
   116→- AC-2: A file containing only YAML comments is treated as valid YAML.
   117→- AC-3: A file containing only whitespace is treated as valid YAML.
   118→- AC-4: The command does not crash or produce a stack trace for any of these edge cases.
   119→
   120→### FR-005: No New Dependencies
   121→**Priority**: Must Have
   122→**User Type**: Project Maintainers
   123→**Requirement**: The validator must be implemented using only the existing project dependencies (Bun built-ins, TypeScript). No new entries may be added to `dependencies` or `devDependencies` in `package.json`.
   124→**Rationale**: The project follows a zero-external-dependency philosophy. The feature request explicitly states "without adding new deps."
   125→**Acceptance Criteria**:
   126→- AC-1: The `package.json` file has no new entries in `dependencies` or `devDependencies` after the feature is implemented.
   127→- AC-2: No `node_modules` additions beyond what already exists.
   128→
   129→### FR-006: Validate Common YAML Constructs
   130→**Priority**: Should Have
   131→**User Type**: Developer
   132→**Requirement**: The validator should correctly identify the validity of common YAML constructs including key-value mappings, sequences (lists), nested structures, quoted strings, multi-line strings (literal and folded block scalars), and comments.
   133→**Rationale**: These are the most frequently used YAML features in configuration files, and the validator must handle them to be practically useful.
   134→**Acceptance Criteria**:
   135→- AC-1: A file with nested key-value mappings is correctly validated.
   136→- AC-2: A file with sequences (both block and flow style) is correctly validated.
   137→- AC-3: A file with multi-line strings (using `|` or `>`) is correctly validated.
   138→- AC-4: A file with inline comments is correctly validated.
   139→
   140→## 6. Non-Functional Requirements
   141→
   142→### 6.1 Performance Expectations
   143→
   144→| Expectation | Target |
   145→|-------------|--------|
   146→| Validation of a file under 1000 lines | Completes in under 1 second |
   147→| Validation of a file under 100 lines | Completes in under 200 milliseconds |
   148→
   149→### 6.2 Security Requirements
   150→
   151→- The command must only read the file specified; it must not write to, modify, or delete any files.
   152→- The command must not execute or evaluate any content within the YAML file.
   153→
   154→### 6.3 Usability Requirements
   155→
   156→- The command must provide a `--help` flag (or equivalent) that describes usage.
   157→- Error messages must be written in plain language, not raw parser internals.
   158→- Output should be suitable for terminal display (no excessive verbosity for valid files).
   159→
   160→### 6.4 Compliance Requirements
   161→
   162→- No additional compliance requirements beyond the zero-dependency constraint.
   163→
   164→## 7. User Stories
   165→
   166→### STORY-001: Validate a Configuration File
   167→**As a** developer
   168→**I want to** run a command that checks my YAML configuration file for syntax errors
   169→**So that** I can catch mistakes before they cause failures in my application or deployment pipeline.
   170→
   171→**Acceptance Scenarios**:
   172→- GIVEN a YAML file with correct syntax, WHEN I run the validator command with the file path, THEN I see a message confirming the file is valid and the process exits with code 0.
   173→- GIVEN a YAML file with a missing colon after a key, WHEN I run the validator command with the file path, THEN I see an error message indicating the line and nature of the problem and the process exits with a non-zero code.
   174→
   175→### STORY-002: Gate a CI Pipeline on YAML Validity
   176→**As a** CI/CD pipeline
   177→**I want to** invoke the YAML validator and use its exit code to determine if configuration files are correct
   178→**So that** deployments are blocked when configuration files contain syntax errors.
   179→
   180→**Acceptance Scenarios**:
   181→- GIVEN a valid YAML configuration file, WHEN the validator is invoked in a pipeline step, THEN the step succeeds (exit code 0).
   182→- GIVEN an invalid YAML configuration file, WHEN the validator is invoked in a pipeline step, THEN the step fails (non-zero exit code) and the error details are visible in the pipeline log.
   183→
   184→### STORY-003: Get Help on Command Usage
   185→**As a** developer unfamiliar with the tool
   186→**I want to** see usage instructions when I pass a help flag
   187→**So that** I understand how to invoke the validator correctly.
   188→
   189→**Acceptance Scenarios**:
   190→- GIVEN no file argument or a `--help` flag, WHEN I run the validator command, THEN I see a usage message describing how to provide a file path.
   191→
   192→## 8. Business Rules
   193→
   194→| Rule ID | Rule | Rationale |
   195→|---------|------|-----------|
   196→| BR-001 | The project must not gain any new runtime or development dependencies | Aligns with the project's zero-dependency philosophy and the explicit feature constraint |
   197→| BR-002 | The validator only checks syntax, not semantic correctness | Keeps scope focused and implementation feasible without external schema libraries |
   198→| BR-003 | Empty YAML documents are considered valid | Per the YAML specification, an empty document is a valid YAML document |
   199→
   200→## 9. Dependencies & Constraints
   201→
   202→| Dependency / Constraint | Type | Impact |
   203→|-------------------------|------|--------|
   204→| Bun runtime | Platform | The command runs under Bun; must use Bun-compatible APIs for file I/O and process management |
   205→| No external YAML parsing library | Constraint | The YAML validation logic must be implemented from scratch or using only built-in capabilities |
   206→| Existing project patterns | Constraint | New code must follow established naming conventions (camelCase functions, kebab-case files, PascalCase types), testing patterns (co-located `*.test.ts`), and error handling style (try/catch with descriptive messages) |
   207→
   208→## 10. Clarifications Log
   209→
   210→| # | Question | Resolution | Source |
   211→|---|----------|------------|--------|
   212→| 1 | What YAML specification version should be targeted? | YAML 1.2 core schema at a practical level; exhaustive compliance not required for MVP | Inferred -- industry standard |
